summary: Evelyn Castillo, who runs youth art workshops at the Marigold Art Centre, describes how the program launched on September 15, 2023 with help from philanthropist Jackson Li, who backed the conversion of an old warehouse. The centre offers traditional and digital arts classes, partners with local schools, and has changed the lives of children like Maria, Alex, Tony and Sofia. She also covers funding challenges and the World Art Workshop, and hopes the program will cultivate empathetic, well-rounded individuals.
one_line: Evelyn Castillo recounts how the Marigold Art Centre's youth art program, launched in 2023, nurtures creativity, inclusion and cultural understanding in local children.
key_facts: The Marigold Art Centre launched its youth programs on September 15, 2023.
Evelyn Castillo is one of the people who run the youth art workshops and classes at the Marigold Art Centre.
Evelyn Castillo founded the youth initiative because she was dissatisfied with dwindling arts programs in schools.
Jackson Li, a local philanthropist and art enthusiast, provided financial backing and community influence for the youth initiative.
Evelyn Castillo and Jackson Li renovated an old warehouse into the learning space, aimed particularly at youth on the fringes with little access to art outlets.
The curriculum includes painting and sculpture as well as digital arts and animation.
Teenager Alex, who had been suspended from school several times for graffiti, joined the Urban Art class and produced mural projects that adorn the town's underpasses.
Tony, diagnosed with autism, excels in the centre's photography classes and has earned accolades in local galleries.
The centre partnered with Elm High School art teacher Ms. Hannah Torres on joint showcases blending academic learning and community engagement.
Funding was a constant obstacle; the centre responded with crowd-funding campaigns and local art fairs with business sponsors.
The World Art Workshop began in October 2023, and children explored traditions from around the globe.
Sofia, whose family immigrated from Mexico, shared Día de los Muertos through her art for a classroom of young Americans.
Eight-year-old Maria, initially shy and reserved, produced a colorful canvas in the early sessions.
